description_ru: Размышление о том, как погоня за эффективностью во всём, от сна до отдыха, лишает жизнь радости и случайности.
text:
A friend of mine, whom I shall call Daniel because he would be mortified to be identified, recently told me that he had stopped enjoying his Sundays. This surprised me, because Daniel is the kind of person who appears to have his life under control. He wakes at the same hour every morning, tracks his sleep with a ring on his finger, logs every kilometre he runs and reads thirty pages of a self-improvement book before breakfast. The trouble, he explained, was that on Sundays he felt obliged to relax efficiently. "If I'm going to rest," he said, with an entirely straight face, "I want to make sure that I'm doing it properly."

It was a funny remark, and I laughed, but it stayed with me for days. Daniel had stumbled upon something that I now consider one of the defining pathologies of our time: the belief that every part of life, however private or pleasurable, should be measured, improved and made more productive. We optimise our diets, our commutes, our friendships and our hobbies. We read summaries instead of books because they save time, listen to podcasts at double speed and schedule "quality time" with our children as though it were a meeting. And in the process, I fear, we are squeezing out the very things that make the effort worthwhile.

Let me be careful here, because I am not an enemy of efficiency. Good systems are a blessing. I am grateful for the engineers who optimised the supply chain that delivers antibiotics to my local pharmacy, and I would not wish to return to a world without timetables, checklists or sensible budgets. When the goal is clear, the means are mechanical and the stakes are high, optimisation is exactly what we need. Nobody wants a surgeon who improvises.

The difficulty arises when we carry that logic into domains where the goal is not clear, or where the process itself is the goal. A walk is not a failed attempt to reach the shops. A conversation with an old friend is not a defective method of exchanging information. A holiday is not an inefficient way of recharging one's productivity, and yet we routinely justify rest by its benefits to work, as if leisure were a kind of maintenance contract for the self. Once we do this, we have quietly accepted that the purpose of a human life is output.

There is an economic phrase for what goes wrong, which is Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The ring on Daniel's finger gives him a score for his sleep every morning, and he told me, rather shamefacedly, that a low score now makes him anxious, and the anxiety makes the next night worse. He has become an unwilling expert in the insomnia produced by monitoring insomnia. The metric, which was meant to serve him, has quietly become his master.

The same pattern can be found everywhere. Teachers, pressed to raise test scores, teach to the test and drain the pleasure from learning. Hospitals, pressed to reduce waiting times, discharge patients prematurely. Social media platforms, designed to maximise engagement, optimise so successfully for our attention that they leave us feeling hollow. In each case, a narrow number has replaced a broad purpose, and the people involved, who are generally conscientious and intelligent, find themselves complicit in a result that none of them wanted.

What is lost, above all, is slack. A system with no spare capacity may be brilliant on paper, but it cannot absorb a surprise, whether a train strike or a sudden illness. The same is true of a life. The unscheduled hour is where we notice a neighbour in distress, where we wander into a bookshop and discover the author who will change our thinking, or where we drift into a conversation that lasts until midnight. Serendipity cannot be put in a calendar, and a diary that is full to the margins has no room for the unexpected.

I am also troubled by what perpetual optimisation does to our attitude to failure. If everything must be done in the best possible way, then every mistake becomes a personal indictment. I notice this in younger colleagues, who often seem afraid to try anything without first reading five guides on the correct method. Yet most of the things we eventually do well, from cooking to writing to parenting, we learn by doing them badly, and with a certain amount of cheerful waste. Amateurs are not only people who lack skill; the word, after all, comes from the Latin for "lover".

So what is the remedy? I do not suggest that we should burn our calendars or flush our fitness trackers down the toilet. I propose a modest discipline of exemptions: a few activities that we deliberately refuse to improve. Choose a hobby at which you will never be good and keep it that way. Take a route home that is longer, for no reason at all. Read a book slowly, or abandon it halfway without guilt. Let one meal per week be thoroughly mediocre and enjoyed anyway.

When I told Daniel all this, he listened politely and then asked me, in all sincerity, whether I had a framework for it. I confess that I laughed again, and so did he, and for a moment I thought I saw something loosen in his shoulders. A fortnight later he sent me a photograph of a lopsided clay bowl that he had made at a pottery class. It was, he admitted, spectacularly bad. He had never looked happier.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Кончик языка между зубами, голос включён: that, the. Не заменяйте на з или д.
Язык поднят, но не касается нёба; губы чуть вытянуты. Нет раскатистого русского р.
Скользящий звук от а к и: life, time. Не обрывайте на а.
optimiSAtion, efFIciency: ударение стоит перед суффиксами -ation и -ency, а не на первом слоге.

questions.question: What did Daniel say about relaxing on Sundays?
questions.answer: He wanted to relax efficiently, to do it properly.

questions.question: What is Goodhart's law?
questions.answer: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

questions.question: What does the writer say is lost in a fully optimised life?
questions.answer: Slack, spare time and the unexpected.

questions.question: What does the writer suggest as a remedy?
questions.answer: Keeping some activities that we deliberately refuse to improve.
